title: Word Break
description: Decide whether a string can be segmented into a sequence of dictionary words.
statement:
A search engine tokenises text using a fixed vocabulary.

You are given a string `s` and a vocabulary of words. Report whether **all** of `s` can be cut into consecutive pieces, where every piece is a word from the vocabulary. Word reuse is unlimited and pieces must cover the string completely, with no gaps and no leftovers.

Greedily taking the longest matching word at each position is not correct: a prefix may match a word and still leave a suffix that cannot be segmented, while a shorter choice would have succeeded. Tracking which prefixes are reachable makes the decision exact.

The vocabulary may be empty, in which case only an empty string could be segmented - and since the string is never empty, the answer is `false`.
inputFormat:
The input is read from standard input:

1. Line 1: the string `s` - lowercase ASCII letters only, never empty (`1 <= length <= 300`). Read the whole line.
2. Line 2: integer `n` - the number of vocabulary words (`0 <= n <= 1000`).
3. Lines 3 to n+2: one vocabulary word per line, lowercase ASCII letters. The vocabulary may contain duplicates.
outputFormat: Print a single line containing the lowercase word `true` if `s` can be fully segmented into vocabulary words, otherwise the lowercase word `false`.
constraints: s and every word use lowercase ASCII letters only
A quadratic table of reachable prefixes is fast enough; substring comparison cost is ignored
notes: Duplicate vocabulary entries change nothing, and a vocabulary word longer than `s` can never be used. `n = 0` is legal and always yields `false`. `abab` with the vocabulary `aba bab` is the classic trap: taking the longest matching word first leaves the single character `b` stranded, while the correct split is `ab` + `ab`. Storing the vocabulary in a hash set keeps the inner membership test constant time.
